name: Ad-hoc Polymorphism (Overloading & Typeclasses)
problem: How can a polymorphic function or operator exhibit distinct implementations depending on argument types without unsafe casting or combinatorial explosion?

origin.summary: The mechanism is documented; first inventor, year and priority are not asserted here.

mechanism: Ad is one family of answers to reusing behavior across representations. The implementation determines what is checked, when it is checked, and which representation crosses the boundary.
costs: The chosen enforcement point moves cost between runtime, compiler, author and operator.
A guarantee applies only within its documented boundary and escape hatches.
transferRule: When another language presents ad, first identify its enforcement boundary and then compare the same failure case.
confidence: MEDIUM: mechanism and transfer prompt are editorially grounded; historical origin and most language cells remain explicitly unresolved.
examples: Worked trace: start with an operation involving ad; record inputs, representation, enforcement point, successful result and the first observable failure.
counterexamples: A language can expose syntax resembling ad while implementing a different semantic guarantee; inspect its specification before transferring conclusions.

assessment.prompt: Compare two languages' treatment of ad for one failing example. What is guaranteed, who pays, and what crosses the boundary?
rubric: Name the concrete problem and two solution choices.
Trace enforcement and failure rather than citing syntax alone.
State one cost and one limitation with evidence.

C.mechanism: C lacks function and operator overloading. Every function symbol requires a unique external linkage name. C11 (§6.5.1.1) provides _Generic compile-time macro selection based on controlling expression type.
C.why: Preserves predictable ABI symbol linkage without name mangling and maintains a minimal one-pass compiler.
C.useWhen: Use _Generic macros when wrapping type-differentiated library primitives (e.g., tgmath.h).
C.price: Macro expansion complexity, opaque compiler diagnostics, and inability to dispatch dynamically on multiple arguments.

C++.mechanism: Function and operator overloading resolved at compile time via Overload Resolution (ISO C++ §16.4), ranking viable candidates across conversions, template specialization, and C++20 requires constraints.
C++.why: Enables expressive mathematical types, generic algorithm specialization, and zero-runtime-cost abstraction.
C++.useWhen: When creating domain types, custom mathematical operators, or generic libraries requiring compile-time dispatch.
C++.price: Complex ABI name mangling, subtle overload ambiguities, fragile SFINAE diagnostics, and template code bloat.

Rust.mechanism: Ad-hoc polymorphism is strictly scoped via Traits (trait, impl Trait for Type). Static dispatch uses monomorphization (impl Trait); dynamic dispatch uses trait objects (dyn Trait fat pointers: data_ptr + vtable_ptr).
Rust.why: Rejects arbitrary function overloading to prevent ambiguity and preserve type inference while enforcing explicit interface contracts.
Rust.useWhen: Use traits for shared behavior across distinct types, preferring static generics unless heterogeneous collections require dyn Trait.
Rust.price: Monomorphization causes binary code bloat and longer compile times; dyn Trait incurs indirect pointer calls and vtable overhead.

Zig.mechanism: Zig deliberately omits function and operator overloading (No hidden control flow, no operator overloading). Ad-hoc dispatch is explicit via comptime type parameters with @typeInfo() or explicit struct vtables.
Zig.why: Ensures reading code reveals exact control flow and instruction costs without hidden compiler-selected overloads.
Zig.useWhen: Use comptime type inspection for compile-time generic dispatch, or explicit struct method tables for runtime interfaces (e.g. std.mem.Allocator).
Zig.price: Requires manual dispatch boilerplate; mathematical operator overloading is unsupported.

Java.mechanism: Method overloading resolved at compile time based on static parameter types; method overriding dispatched dynamically at runtime via invokevirtual (vtable) or invokeinterface (itable). No user operator overloading.
Java.why: Balances class-based polymorphism with JVM bytecode predictability, avoiding complex operator overloading pitfalls.
Java.useWhen: When providing ergonomic API method variants accepting different argument types or counts.
Java.price: Compile-time static binding can lead to subtle bugs when overloaded methods interact with overriding; autoboxing overhead.

C#.mechanism: Compile-time method and operator overloading (ECMA-334 §12.6.3). C# 11 introduced static abstract members in interfaces enabling generic math and typeclass-like ad-hoc polymorphism.
C#.why: Enables idiomatic numerical programming and flexible method overloading while integrating with CLI runtime generics.
C#.useWhen: When overloading methods for different types or implementing generic mathematical algorithms via static interface contracts.
C#.price: Complex overload resolution rules, boxing of value types when passed to non-generic interfaces, and IL metadata growth.

Kotlin.mechanism: Method overloading resolved at compile time plus a fixed set of overloadable operator conventions (operator fun plus, get, invoke).
Kotlin.why: Allows safe, bounded operator ergonomics without arbitrary user operator definitions.
Kotlin.useWhen: When creating domain-specific DSLs, collection accessors, or mathematical types.
Kotlin.price: Name collision risks in operator extensions; compile-time overload resolution complexity.

Swift.mechanism: Function and operator overloading resolved at compile time; Protocol-oriented polymorphism dispatched via Protocol Witness Tables (PWT) for generics or existential containers for dynamic values.
Swift.why: Enables protocol-oriented architecture with high-performance static optimization and value semantics.
Swift.useWhen: Use protocols and generics for type-safe polymorphic contracts; use any Protocol only for heterogeneous storage.
Swift.price: Existential containers exceeding 3 words trigger heap allocation; witness table lookups incur pointer indirection.

Go.mechanism: Go explicitly omits function and operator overloading. Polymorphism is achieved via structural interfaces (two-word iface: itab + data pointer) or Go 1.18+ type parameters with type sets.
Go.why: Prioritizes readability and simplicity; having multiple functions with identical names was considered confusing in large codebases.
Go.useWhen: Use distinct function names (e.g. NewReader, NewReaderSize) or structural interfaces to accept polymorphic behaviors.
Go.price: Cannot overload operators for custom numerical types; verbose explicit function names.

Python.mechanism: Dynamic operator ad-hoc polymorphism via dunder methods (__add__, __mul__). Function overloading is not syntactic (subsequent def overwrites), but functools.singledispatch provides runtime type dispatch.
Python.why: Preserves Python dynamic object model and duck typing while allowing operator customization.
Python.useWhen: Implement dunder methods for custom classes emulating numeric or container behavior.
Python.price: Runtime dictionary lookup overhead for method calls; lack of compile-time signature verification.

JavaScript.mechanism: JavaScript has no static function or operator overloading. Functions accept dynamic arity/types inspected via typeof, instanceof, or rest arguments.
JavaScript.why: Conforms to dynamic, untyped scripting runtime design.
JavaScript.useWhen: Use argument inspection and default parameters to handle varied input types.
JavaScript.price: Manual branching boilerplate in function bodies; JIT deoptimization if call-site argument types fluctuate.

TypeScript.mechanism: Compile-time overload signatures checked by the type system; a single implementation body handles all cases with runtime type narrowing. Overloads are fully erased at compile time.
TypeScript.why: Provides type-safe caller ergonomics on top of existing JavaScript idioms without altering runtime semantics.
TypeScript.useWhen: When an existing function accepts distinct argument combinations yielding distinct return types.
TypeScript.price: Implementation signature must be manually generalized; runtime type narrowing code is still required.

Dart.mechanism: Supports operator overloading (operator +), but deliberately omits method overloading to preserve optional typing and avoid overload ambiguity (uses named optional parameters).
Dart.why: Avoids brittle overload resolution cascades in an optionally typed sound type system.
Dart.useWhen: Overload operators for custom mathematical types; use named optional parameters for varied method signatures.
Dart.price: Cannot overload methods by parameter type; requires distinct method names or named parameters.

Ruby.mechanism: Operators are syntactic sugar for method calls (def +(other)); method overloading does not exist natively but is emulated via dynamic typing, splat arguments, or keyword parameters.
Ruby.why: Adheres to pure object-oriented message passing principles where everything is an object receiving messages.
Ruby.useWhen: Define operator methods on domain models to provide expressive, fluent domain syntax.
Ruby.price: Dynamic method lookup overhead via method cache; potential name collision from monkey patching.

PHP.mechanism: PHP does not support signature-based function overloading. Overloading is emulated dynamically via magic methods (__call, __callStatic) or union types and type checking.
PHP.why: Historical single-pass execution model; maintains backward compatibility with dynamic scripting roots.
PHP.useWhen: Use union types in method signatures or __call magic methods for dynamic delegation.
PHP.price: Performance cost of magic method interception; lack of IDE autocompletion without docblocks.

Haskell.mechanism: Type Classes (class, instance), the canonical foundation of ad-hoc polymorphism (Wadler & Blott 1989). Lowered by GHC into implicit dictionary passing, eliminated via monomorphization when types are known.
Haskell.why: Integrates principled ad-hoc polymorphism into Hindley-Milner type inference without ambiguous type annotations.
Haskell.useWhen: Whenever defining shared operations across algebraic data types (e.g. Eq, Ord, Show, Functor, Monad).
Haskell.price: Dictionary passing adds pointer indirection unless GHC specializes and inlines the instance; coherence restrictions.

OCaml.mechanism: OCaml deliberately omits ad-hoc polymorphism and function/operator overloading to preserve complete, decidable Hindley-Milner type inference. Operators are monomorphic (+ vs +.). Emulated via first-class modules.
OCaml.why: Guarantees principal type inference: the compiler never requires type annotations to resolve overloaded operations.
OCaml.useWhen: Use first-class modules or explicit function passing when polymorphic behavior is needed across representations.
OCaml.price: Requires distinct operator symbols (+., *. ) and explicit module passing boilerplate.

Erlang/Elixir.mechanism: Erlang uses arity-based dispatch (foo/1 vs foo/2) and pattern matching guards. Elixir adds Protocols (defprotocol, defimpl) providing fast dynamic polymorphism dispatched on the data type.
Erlang/Elixir.why: Fits concurrent actor message-passing and immutable functional data transformations.
Erlang/Elixir.useWhen: Use Elixir protocols for extensible data type contracts (e.g. Enumerable, String.Chars).
Erlang/Elixir.price: Dynamic protocol dispatch table lookup; Erlang arity dispatch cannot distinguish types with identical arity.

Lisp/Clojure.mechanism: Common Lisp CLOS provides multi-argument dynamic dispatch (defgeneric/defmethod). Clojure provides defmulti/defmethod (arbitrary dispatch fn) and defprotocol (fast JVM interface dispatch).
Lisp/Clojure.why: Decouples operations from data type hierarchies, allowing extension without modifying original types.
Lisp/Clojure.useWhen: Use defprotocol for high-performance polymorphic dispatch on type; use defmulti for complex value-based dispatch.
Lisp/Clojure.price: Multimethod dispatch involves hash table lookups; protocol dispatch is single-dispatch on first argument.

Smalltalk.mechanism: Pure polymorphic message dispatch (#message:with:). Different receiver classes handle identical selectors differently. Multi-type operations employ double dispatch.
Smalltalk.why: Foundational object-oriented design where objects communicate solely through late-bound message sending.
Smalltalk.useWhen: When creating polymorphic domain objects responding to common message selectors.
Smalltalk.price: Dynamic message lookup overhead (mitigated by inline caching in modern VMs); double dispatch boilerplate for binary operators.

Prolog.mechanism: Predicates are identified by Name/Arity. Polymorphism across distinct argument types is achieved via unification across multiple clauses matching different compound terms.
Prolog.why: Relational logic programming paradigm based on Robinson unification and backtracking.
Prolog.useWhen: Define multiple clauses matching different term structures to handle varied representations.
Prolog.price: Backtracking overhead if clauses are not mutually exclusive or indexed on the first argument.

APL/J.mechanism: Primitive verbs exhibit monadic (unary) or dyadic (binary) ad-hoc behaviors based on valence. J allows explicit verb : 0 valence-based definitions.
APL/J.why: Maximizes notation density and concise mathematical array manipulation.
APL/J.useWhen: When defining array operations that behave as a transformation on one operand or a combination on two.
APL/J.price: Steep learning curve; limited to valence-based overloading rather than arbitrary type-based resolution.

Forth.mechanism: Forth maintains a monomorphic dictionary where each word has a single execution token. Overloading is omitted to preserve stack contract predictability and interpreter simplicity.
Forth.why: Minimalist stack machine philosophy where words operate on raw untyped stack cells.
Forth.useWhen: Use distinct words with descriptive prefixes (e.g. + for integers, F+ for floats).
Forth.price: Programmer must manually select correct word based on operand type.

SQL.mechanism: SQL:1999+ routines and operators can be overloaded by argument data types. The query planner resolves candidates using type conversion hierarchies and precedence rules.
SQL.why: Allows database functions and operators to work naturally across various numeric, text, and temporal column types.
SQL.useWhen: Creating user-defined functions or custom domain operators in stored procedures.
SQL.price: Ambiguous function resolution errors during complex implicit type casting.

Ada.mechanism: Subprograms and operators support overloading resolved at compile time using both argument types and expected return types (bidirectional overload resolution).
Ada.why: Enforces high-integrity systems engineering where strong typing and clear operator semantics coexist.
Ada.useWhen: When defining domain-specific numerical types or abstract data types requiring standard arithmetic operators.
Ada.price: Compiler compilation time and complex ambiguity errors if return type context is underspecified.

Scala.mechanism: Method overloading plus Scala 3 contextual abstractions (trait, given, using) and extension methods implementing typeclasses, resolved at compile time via implicit dictionary passing.
Scala.why: Unifies object-oriented subtyping with principled functional ad-hoc polymorphism.
Scala.useWhen: Use given/using typeclasses for ad-hoc extension; use method overloading for straightforward API ergonomics.
Scala.price: Compile time overhead from implicit search; potential given priority conflicts.
